```{r}
#| label: packages
#| code-fold: false
#| collapse: true
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(sf)
library(usmap)
library(here)
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(ggforce)
```

## Data
### Error data

In addition to reading in the data, I calculate trees per acre. This depends on whether the tree was measured in a subplot, microplot, or macroplot. 

```{r}
#| label: read-error-data
#| code-fold: false

trees_err <- readRDS(here('data', 'sim_outputs', 'all_IE_uncalib_err.RDS')) |>
  filter(calib_use) |>
  mutate(macro = NUM_PLOTS != 4,
         TPA_1 = case_when(fia_dbh_1 < 5 ~ 74.965282,
                           !macro&fia_dbh_1 >= 5 ~ 6.018046,
                           macro&fia_dbh_1 >= 5 ~ 0.999188,
                           .default = NA),
         TPA_2 = case_when(fia_dbh_2 < 5 ~ 74.965282,
                           !macro&fia_dbh_2 >= 5 ~ 6.018046,
                           macro&fia_dbh_2 >= 5 ~ 0.999188,
                           .default = NA),
         rm = fia_dg == 0)
head(trees_err)
```

Instead of going with the default alphabetical factor ordering, I'll order the "species" factor in the dataframe in order of species prevalence.

```{r}
#| label: species-factor
#| code-fold: false

sp_table <- sort(table(trees_err$common_name), decreasing = TRUE)
knitr::kable(sp_table, col.names = c('Species', 'Frequency'))
trees_err$common_name <- factor(trees_err$common_name, 
                                levels = names(sp_table),
                                ordered = TRUE)
sp_group_table <- sort(table(trees_err$fvs_sp_group), decreasing = TRUE)
trees_err$fvs_sp_group <- factor(trees_err$fvs_sp_group, 
                                 levels = names(sp_group_table),
                                 ordered = TRUE)
```

I'll also define 4 study species to focus on. Douglas-fir is the most common species in the study region, it's widespread, and it's commercially important (though perhaps more so in the PNW than the inland northwest). Lodgepole pine is also quite common, and it spans an elevational gradient, which makes it a useful case study to look at some elevational effects. Western larch is more specialized to somewhat wetter areas. Finally, ponderosa pine is more restricted to dry sites than the other species, so trends in FVS' PIPO accuracy may give some insight into dry site accuracy.

```{r}
#| label: def-study-sp
#| code-fold: false
study_sps <- c('Douglas-fir', 'lodgepole pine', 
               'western larch',  'ponderosa pine')
```

The initial tree dataframe is structured where every row is a tree. However, sometimes we may want to instead look at error at the species-within-stand level, and sometimes just at the stand level. I took the median of all metrics because they are quite skewed, so the mean is not as accurate a representation of the center of the distribution. The `matched_by` column describes how the habitat type was matched.

```{r}
#| label: stand-err
#| collapse: true
#| code-fold: false

stand_err <- readRDS(here('data', 'sim_outputs', 'all_IE_uncalib_err.RDS')) |>
  filter(!died, !broke, !started_broken) |>
  group_by(CID) |>
  summarize(med_dbh1 = median(fia_dbh_1),
            med_ht1 = median(fia_ht_1),
            med_dbh2 = median(fia_dbh_2),
            med_ht2 = median(fia_ht_2),
            med_dg = median(fia_dg),
            med_hg = median(fia_hg),
            med_dds = median(fia_dds),
            med_dg_err = median(dg_err),
            med_hg_err = median(hg_err),
            med_ldds_err = median(ldds_err)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # want to get plot information back
  left_join(distinct(trees_err[c('CID', 'LATITUDE', 'LONGITUDE',
                                 'EMAP_HEX',  'LOCATION', 'ECOREGION', 
                                 'AGE', 'ASPECT', 'SLOPE', 'ELEVFT', 'PV_CODE', 
                                 'dominant_sp', 'matched_by', 'OWNCD')]))
head(stand_err)

stand_sp_err <- readRDS(here('data', 'sim_outputs', 'all_IE_uncalib_err.RDS')) |>
  filter(!died, !broke, !started_broken) |>
  group_by(CID, fvs_sp, common_name) |>
  summarize(med_dbh1 = median(fia_dbh_1),
            med_ht1 = median(fia_ht_1),
            med_dbh2 = median(fia_dbh_2),
            med_ht2 = median(fia_ht_2),
             med_dg = median(fia_dg),
            med_hg = median(fia_hg),
            med_dds = median(fia_dds),
            med_dg_err = median(dg_err),
            med_hg_err = median(hg_err),
            med_ldds_err = median(ldds_err)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # want to get plot information back
  left_join(distinct(trees_err[c('CID', 'LATITUDE', 'LONGITUDE',
                                 'EMAP_HEX',  'LOCATION', 'ECOREGION', 
                                 'AGE', 'ASPECT', 'SLOPE', 'ELEVFT', 'PV_CODE',
                                 'OWNCD',
                                 'dominant_sp', 'matched_by')]))
head(stand_sp_err)
```

Finally, a color palette:

```{r}
#| label: color-pal
#| code-fold: false
spectral_plus <- c(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(11, 'Spectral'), '#aaa', '#aaa')
```

### Spatial Data

This is primarily for context when mapping.

```{r}
#| label: read-spatial
#| code-fold: false
#| collapse: true

variants <- here('raw_data', 'FVSVariantMap20210525', 
                         'FVS_Variants_and_Locations.shp') |>
  st_read() |>
  filter(FVSVariant != 'AK') |>
  mutate(ie_locs = factor(ifelse(FVSVariant == 'IE'|FVSVariant == 'EM', FVSLocName, NA))) |>
  group_by(ie_locs, FVSVariant) |>
  summarize() |>
  ungroup()

ie <- filter(variants, FVSVariant == 'IE') |>
  select(geometry) |>
  summarize()

ie_buffered <- st_buffer(ie, dist = 100*1000) |>
  st_intersection(variants) |># don't want to go up into Canada
  summarize() |>
  st_convex_hull()
epa_hexes <- st_read(here('raw_data', 
                          'FIA_Forest_Biomass_Estimates_1873',
                          'data',
                          'CONUSbiohex2020.shp')) |>
  select(EMAP_HEX, geometry) |>
  st_transform(crs = st_crs(variants))

ie_hexes <- epa_hexes |>
  st_filter(ie_buffered,
            .predicate = st_intersects)

states <- usmap::us_map(regions = 'states', include = c('ID', 'MT', 'OR', 'WA')) |>
  st_transform(crs = st_crs(ie_buffered))
```

And the locations of a few towns/cities for context.

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
missoula <- st_as_sf(data.frame(lat = 46.872890, lon = -114.004997),
                     coords = c('lon', 'lat'),
                     crs = 'epsg:4326')
spokane <- st_as_sf(data.frame(lat = 47.658779, lon = -117.436048),
                    coords = c('lon', 'lat'),
                    crs = 'epsg:4326')
moscow <- st_as_sf(data.frame(lat = 46.731705, lon = -116.999939),
                  coords = c('lon', 'lat'),
                  crs = 'epsg:4326')
```

## Visualizing Error

### Error distributions

```{r}
#| label: error_dists
dg_err_dist <- trees_err |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_histogram(aes(x = dg_err), color = 'black', fill = 'lightgrey')+
  labs(x = 'Diameter growth error (in)',
       y = 'Count')

hg_err_dist <- trees_err |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_histogram(aes(x = hg_err), color = 'black', fill = 'lightgrey')+
  labs(x = 'Height growth error (in)',
       y = 'Count')

ldds_err_dist <- trees_err |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_histogram(aes(x = ldds_err), color = 'black', fill = 'lightgrey')+
  labs(x = 'log(DDS) growth error',
       y = 'Count')

dg_err_dist+hg_err_dist+ldds_err_dist&theme_bw()&geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0))
```

Diameter growth errors are generally small but the center of the distribution is less than 0, indicating general overprediction of diameter growth. Height error is much more variable (see scale of x-axis) and again appears to be slightly off-center, though it's hard to tell. Height error may be a little skewed, but both look relatively normal which is a good sign because that is an FVS assumption. In contrast log(DDS) growth error is more skewed, with a longer tail to the left of the mode of the distribution.

The joint diameter and height error distribution is also worth looking it. However, there are some trees with extremely large errors that make the joint picture "zoomed out," so we'll do a version with those removed by filtering out observations outside of the 1.5*IQR range. I'll also scale the axes by SD so that they're on comparable scales and I can use a fixed aspect ratio to better look at the shape of the joint distribution without it being confounded with the different scales of the variables.

```{r}
survivors_summ <- trees_err |>
  summarize(dg_lquant = quantile(dg_err, 0.25),
            dg_uquant = quantile(dg_err, 0.75),
            hg_lquant = quantile(hg_err, 0.25),
            hg_uquant = quantile(hg_err, 0.75),
            ldds_lquant = quantile(ldds_err, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
            ldds_uquant = quantile(ldds_err, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE))
survivors_summ$dg_iqr <- survivors_summ$dg_uquant-survivors_summ$dg_lquant
survivors_summ$hg_iqr <- survivors_summ$hg_uquant-survivors_summ$hg_lquant
survivors_summ$ldds_iqr <- survivors_summ$ldds_uquant-survivors_summ$ldds_lquant

trees_err |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_density_2d_filled(aes(x = dg_err/sd(dg_err), y = hg_err/sd(hg_err)))+
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), color = 'lightgrey', linetype = 'dashed')+
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0), color = 'lightgrey', linetype = 'dashed')+
  coord_fixed()+
  labs(x = 'Diameter growth error, sd-scaled',
       y = 'Height growth error, sd-scaled',
       fill = 'Density bin',
       title = 'All alive, unbroken trees')

trees_err |>
  filter(dg_err >= survivors_summ$dg_lquant-1.5*survivors_summ$dg_iqr,
         dg_err <= survivors_summ$dg_uquant+1.5*survivors_summ$dg_iqr,
         hg_err >= survivors_summ$hg_lquant-1.5*survivors_summ$hg_iqr,
         hg_err <= survivors_summ$hg_uquant+1.5*survivors_summ$hg_iqr) |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_density_2d_filled(aes(x = dg_err/sd(dg_err), y = hg_err/sd(hg_err)))+
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), color = 'lightgrey', linetype = 'dashed')+
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0), color = 'lightgrey', linetype = 'dashed')+
  labs(x = 'Diameter growth error, sd-scaled',
       y = 'Height growth error, sd-scaled',
       fill = 'Density bin',
       title = 'Alive, unbroken trees, no outliers')
```

It's possible that the shape of this distribution is created by the species-level relationships between diameter and height growth. So, let's do this again but only for the most common species and split by species. This is also just alive, unbroken trees with outliers removed.

```{r}
trees_err |>
  filter(dg_err >= survivors_summ$dg_lquant-1.5*survivors_summ$dg_iqr,
         dg_err <= survivors_summ$dg_uquant+1.5*survivors_summ$dg_iqr,
         hg_err >= survivors_summ$hg_lquant-1.5*survivors_summ$hg_iqr,
         hg_err <= survivors_summ$hg_uquant+1.5*survivors_summ$hg_iqr,
         common_name %in% study_sps) |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_density_2d_filled(aes(x = dg_err/(sd(dg_err)), y = hg_err/(sd(hg_err))))+
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), color = 'lightgrey', linetype = 'dashed')+
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0), color = 'lightgrey', linetype = 'dashed')+
  facet_wrap(facets = vars(common_name))+
  theme_bw()+
  coord_fixed()+
  labs(x = 'Diameter growth error, sd-scaled',
       y = 'Height growth error, sd-scaled',
       fill = 'Density bin')
```
Splitting it out by species like this shows that the relationship we see in the unsplit version is probably at least somewhat influenced by how species. Yet, most species show a similar pattern. We don't see a bunch of nice, round-looking distributions that when you combine them they make that diagonal blob. Instead, it's a bunch of diagonal blobs that when combined make another diagonal blob. Western larch actually looks pretty good, though it's a bit diffuse.

It's also interesting how much more dense lodgepole error is relative to Doug fir, which is quite a bit more diffuse over the space. It looks like FVS is more consistently wrong with lodgepole than with Doug fir. All this is good to put in our back pocket to consider whether we should be calibrating diameter alone or both, and whether our model should consider both at once. A nice part about this diagonal blob shape is that bringing diameter growth error closer to 0 also brings height growth error closer to 0. As Dave pointed out, if it went the other way but the center of mass was in the same place, bringing diameter growth error from negative towards 0 would make height growth error get worse (more negative).

### Error relationships

This dataframe will be used for adding annotations:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
median_errs <- trees_err |>
  filter(common_name %in% study_sps) |>
  summarize(med_dg_err = median(dg_err), 
            med_hg_err = median(hg_err),
            med_ldds_err = median(ldds_err),
            .by = common_name) |>
  # bounds where growth estimates are weighted
  mutate(weight_lower = case_when(common_name == 'lodgepole pine' ~ 1,
                                  .default = 2),
         weight_upper = case_when(common_name == 'lodgepole pine' ~ 5,
                                  .default = 10))
```

```{r}
#| label: dg-err-vs-dbh1
trees_err |>
  filter(common_name %in% study_sps) |>
  ggplot()+
  # shade in the region where prediction will be influenced by large tree model
  geom_rect(data = median_errs, aes(xmin = weight_lower, xmax = weight_upper,
                                    ymin = -8, ymax = 11),
            fill = 'grey')+
  geom_point(aes(x = fia_dbh_1, y = dg_err, color = common_name),
             alpha = 0.25, size = 0.75)+
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0))+
  # everything to the left of this is a "small tree" and was grown height-first
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 3), lty = 'dotted')+
  geom_hline(data = median_errs, aes(yintercept = med_dg_err),
             linetype = 'dashed')+
  facet_wrap(facets = vars(common_name))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'none',
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA))+
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Dark2')+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-8, 11))+
  labs(x = 'Starting DBH', y = 'Error in diameter growth', color = 'Species')
```

After what I saw with the diameter growth discontinuity, I'll take the pattern of trees < 5" DBH with a grain of salt because it may just be a sample size issue. Generally, it looks like diameter growth error decreases with tree size, and median error is below 0. 

Relative error is also worth looking at. That is, how bad are the errors relative to the actual measurement? For example, a 2-inch difference is pretty bad for a tree that's 5", but not bad for a tree that has a DBH of 40" or more. Based on the error vs starting DBH relationship above, I expect relative error to decrease as starting DBH increases.

```{r}
#| label: rel-dg-err-vs-dbh1

trees_err |>
  filter(common_name %in% study_sps) |>
  mutate(rel_dg_err = 100*abs(dg_err/fia_dbh_2)) |>
  ggplot()+
  # shade in the region where prediction will be influenced by large tree model
  geom_rect(data = median_errs, aes(xmin = weight_lower, xmax = weight_upper,
                                    ymin = 0, ymax = 120),
            fill = 'grey')+
  geom_point(aes(x = fia_dbh_1, y = rel_dg_err, color = common_name),
             alpha = 0.5, size = 1)+
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0))+
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 3), lty = 'dashed')+
  facet_wrap(facets = vars(common_name), scales = 'free_x')+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'none')+
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Dark2')+
  labs(x = 'Starting DBH', y = '% DG error')

```
To reduce the amount of information here, I'll plot just the median relative error at each DBH value for each species so that there is less overplotting.

```{r}
#| label: med-rel-dg-err
trees_err |>
  filter(common_name %in% study_sps) |>
  mutate(rel_dg_err = 100*abs(dg_err/fia_dbh_2)) |>
  summarize(med_err = median(rel_dg_err), .by = c(fia_dbh_1, common_name)) |>
  ggplot()+
  # shade in the region where prediction will be influenced by large tree model
  geom_rect(data = median_errs, aes(xmin = weight_lower, xmax = weight_upper,
                                    ymin = 0, ymax = 120),
            fill = 'grey')+
  geom_point(aes(x = fia_dbh_1, y = med_err, color = common_name),
             alpha = 0.5, size = 1)+
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0))+
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 3), lty = 'dashed')+
  facet_wrap(facets = vars(common_name), scales = 'free')+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'none')+
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Dark2')+
  labs(x = 'Starting DBH', y = 'Median % DG error')
```
I can make the same plots for height error:

```{r}
#| label: htg-err-vs-dbh1
trees_err |>

  # shade in the region where prediction will be influenced by large tree model
  geom_rect(data = median_errs, aes(xmin = weight_lower, xmax = weight_upper,
                                    ymin = -40, ymax = 60),
            fill = 'grey')+
  geom_point(aes(x = fia_dbh_1, y = hg_err, color = common_name),

  # everything to the left of this is a "small tree" and was grown height-first
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 3), lty = 'dotted')+
  geom_hline(data = median_errs, aes(yintercept = med_hg_err),
             linetype = 'dashed')+
  facet_wrap(facets = vars(common_name))+
  theme_bw()+

        panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA))+

```
Height error is much larger and more variable.

```{r}
trees_err |>
  filter(common_name %in% study_sps) |>
  mutate(rel_htg_err = 100*abs(hg_err/fia_ht_2)) |>
 # summarize(med_err = median(rel_htg_err), .by = c(fia_dbh_1, common_name)) |>
  ggplot()+
  # shade in the region where prediction will be influenced by large tree model
  geom_rect(data = median_errs, aes(xmin = weight_lower, xmax = weight_upper,
                                    ymin = 0, ymax = 120),
            fill = 'grey')+
  geom_point(aes(x = fia_dbh_1, y = rel_htg_err, color = common_name),
             alpha = 0.5, size = 1)+

```
Like with DBH error, relative height growth error decreases as trees get larger. I'll do the same thing of plotting the median relative height growth error for each starting DBH and each species, just to make it a bit easier to see the overall patterns here.

```{r}
trees_err |>
  filter(common_name %in% study_sps) |>
  mutate(rel_htg_err = 100*abs(hg_err/fia_ht_2)) |>
  summarize(med_err = median(rel_htg_err), .by = c(fia_dbh_1, common_name)) |>

                                    ymin = 0, ymax = 100),
```

## Mapping

First, need to turn stand-level error measurements into spatial data.

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
stand_err_spat <- st_as_sf(stand_err, coords = c('LONGITUDE', 'LATITUDE'),
                           crs = 'epsg:4269') |>
  st_transform(crs = st_crs(ie_buffered))
stand_sp_err_spat <- st_as_sf(stand_sp_err, coords = c('LONGITUDE', 'LATITUDE'),
                              crs = 'epsg:4269')
```

Now, we can make some maps!

### Habitat types and EPA hexes

```{r}
stand_err_spat |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = 'darkgrey')+
  geom_sf(aes(color = dominant_sp), size = 0.75)+
  geom_sf(data = states, color = 'white', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie, fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie_buffered, linetype = 'dashed', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = missoula, size = 2, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = spokane, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = moscow, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')+
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3)))
```
Same, but as a raster with the majority habitat type filling each cell:

```{r}
template <- terra::rast(nrows = 75, ncols = 75, nlyrs = 1,
                        crs = terra::crs(terra::vect(stand_err_spat)),
                        extent = terra::ext(terra::vect(stand_err_spat)))
habtype_raster <- terra::rasterize(terra::vect(stand_err_spat), template,
                                   field = 'dominant_sp')

ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = 'darkgrey')+
  geom_spatraster(data = habtype_raster)+
  geom_sf(data = states, color = 'white', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie, fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie_buffered, linetype = 'dashed', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = missoula, size = 2, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = spokane, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = moscow, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')+
  scale_fill_discrete(na.value = NA)+
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3)))
  
```



but grouping the less common habitat types together to reduce the number of colors:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
hab_frequencies <- stand_err |>
  group_by(dominant_sp) |>
  tally() |>
  arrange(desc(n))

hab_frequencies

common_habs <- hab_frequencies$dominant_sp[1:6]
```

```{r}
stand_err_spat |>
  mutate(dominant_sp_simple = ifelse(dominant_sp %in% common_habs, dominant_sp, 'other')) |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = 'darkgrey')+
  geom_sf(aes(color = dominant_sp_simple), size = 0.75)+
  geom_sf(data = states, color = 'white', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie, fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie_buffered, linetype = 'dashed', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = missoula, size = 2, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = spokane, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = moscow, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  theme_bw()+
  scale_color_brewer(type = 'qual')+
  theme(legend.key = element_rect(fill = 'darkgrey'),
        legend.position = 'bottom')+
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3)))
  labs(color = 'Dominant species')
```

```{r}
fia_per_hex <- stand_err |>
  distinct(CID, EMAP_HEX) |>
  group_by(EMAP_HEX) |>
  tally() |>
  right_join(ie_hexes) |>
  st_as_sf()
ggplot(fia_per_hex)+
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = 'darkgrey')+
  geom_sf(aes(fill = n))+
  geom_sf(data = states, color = 'white', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie, fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie_buffered, linetype = 'dashed', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = missoula, size = 2, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = spokane, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = moscow, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 5),
                              limits = c(0, 30))+
  labs(fill = '# FIA conditions')+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

```


### Error

These data are certainly best mapped as rasters.

```{r}
template <- terra::rast(nrows = 75, ncols = 75, nlyrs = 1,
                        crs = terra::crs(terra::vect(stand_sp_err_spat)),
                        extent = terra::ext(terra::vect(stand_sp_err_spat)))

dg_err_rast <- rasterize(vect(stand_sp_err_spat), template,
                         field = 'med_dg_err',
                         fun = median)

hg_err_rast <- rasterize(vect(stand_sp_err_spat), template,
                         field = 'med_hg_err',
                         fun = median)

ldds_err_rast <- rasterize(vect(stand_sp_err_spat), template,
                         field = 'med_ldds_err',
                         fun = median)


```


```{r}
ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = 'darkgrey')+
  geom_spatraster(data = ldds_err_rast)+
  geom_sf(data = ie, fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie_buffered, linetype = 'dashed', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = missoula, size = 2, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = spokane, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = moscow, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(na.value = NA)+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')+
  labs(fill = 'Median of stand median ln(DDS) error')
```
Same map, but with height growth error:

```{r}
stand_err_spat |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = 'darkgrey')+
  geom_sf(aes(color = med_hg_err), size = 0.75)+
  geom_sf(data = states, color = 'white', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie, fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie_buffered, linetype = 'dashed', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = missoula, size = 2, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = spokane, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = moscow, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  viridis::scale_color_viridis()+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')+
  labs(color = 'Stand median height growth error')
```

There is a bit of a pattern here, maybe. Height error skews more positive in north Idaho and more negative on the boundaries of the variant. The fact that diameter growth error doesn't have the same spatial patterns makes me think that maybe there is a habitat x diameter growth x height growth miscalibration in FVS.

Splitting it out by species:

```{r}
stand_sp_err_spat |>
  filter(common_name %in% study_sps) |>
  ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = 'darkgrey')+
  geom_sf(aes(color = med_ldds_err), size = 0.75)+
  geom_sf(data = states, color = 'white', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie, fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = ie_buffered, linetype = 'dashed', fill = NA)+
  geom_sf(data = missoula, size = 2, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = spokane, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  geom_sf(data = moscow, size = 1.5, pch = 21, fill = 'white')+
  facet_wrap(facets = vars(common_name))+
  viridis::scale_color_viridis()+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')+
  labs(color = 'Stand median ln(DDS) error')
```

It definitely seems like different species have some different spatial patterns in error. We can also get a sense of species distribution across the study region, which of course I'm always a fan of. It's interesting that error doesn't get worse once we cross the IE variant boundary and enter the buffer zone.
